paragraphs: [The Rabbanites] claim that when God (mighty and exalted) handed the Torah to Moses (peace upon him) at Sinai, He instructed him in its tafāsīr (commentaries) and maʿānī (meanings), and that Moses then taught these to the Children of Israel, expounding them at ʿeber ha-Yarden, as Scripture says (Deut 1:5): "Beyond the Jordan, in the land of Moab, Moses undertook to expound this Torah." Some of them have gone so far as to say that God handed Moses all he would ever need, down to the very amulets.[{2}] They have further argued for the claim that God instructed Moses in the commentaries and meanings of the Torah from Exod 24:12: "Come up to Me on the mountain, and I will give thee the stone tablets, and the Torah, and the commandments, which I have written to teach them." They read the four phrases as a fourfold revelation: "the stone tablets" = the Decalogue; "the Torah" = the [written] Pentateuch; "the commandments" = the Mishnah; "which I have written" = the Talmud. The proponent of this case continues: "Likewise the verse Moses undertook to expound this Torah (Deut 1:5) — by expound he means the Mishnah and Talmud. Moses, peace upon him, gathered the wise men of Israel and made clear to them the meanings of the Torah, and the qal va-ḥomer (a fortiori reasoning), and what is not explained in the Torah except in brief. To this end he said (Deut 1:13): 'Bring me wise and understanding men.' And likewise he warned them in another place (Deut 17:8–10): 'If a matter is too hidden from thee in judgment … then thou shalt arise and go up … and come unto the priests, the Levites … and do according to the sentence that they shall tell thee.' He did not say 'according to what is written in the Torah,' but 'according to the sentence that they declare to thee'; and he said (v. 11): 'Thou shalt not turn aside from the sentence that they shall declare to thee.'" They say: whoever transgresses their word merits death; and whoever opposes them is named "the haughty" (Prov 15:12: "Thou shalt find the haughty unwilling to be admonished, and unwilling to go to the wise"); "the ignorant" (Prov 1:22; 18:2: "The ignorant desire not understanding"; 1:7); and "the heedless" (Prov 14:15: "The heedless believeth every word").

They argue: fiṭna (acumen) is itself wisdom, as Solomon says (Prov 8:12): "I, Wisdom, dwell with acumen." Whoever has wisdom and acumen is far from every wicked path. The heedless fall into trouble, as Solomon says (Prov 22:3): "The acute man sees evil and conceals himself; the heedless pass on and are stricken." They then string together praise of the wise and incitement to wisdom in many passages from Solomon and others — among them (Prov 22:17): "Incline thine ear and hear the words of the wise." They say: exile fell upon the House of Israel only when they abandoned interest in the Talmud called daʿat (knowledge), as Hosea 4:6 says: "My people are destroyed for lack of knowledge"; and Isa 5:13: "Therefore my people are gone into captivity for lack of knowledge"; and Prov 19:2: "That the soul be without knowledge is not good." (Up to this point: hermeneutic and homiletic taʾwīl; no firm argument.)

The proponent then takes up his case more substantively. He says: anyone who differs from the wise — that is, the Rabbanites — is to be told: if you rely only on the written form of the Torah, then you will find the name of the Creator written with the letters yod-he[-vav-he] (= YHWH) — yet you do not read this as it is written; you read it as Adonai.[{3}] Likewise Israel is written with shin but read with sin (i.e., the sin-side of the letter). Likewise shibbolet, Sodom, fistān, sefīdah, fakh[{4}] — each written with shin but read with sin (or vice versa). He goes on: many words in Scripture are written defectively (without the matres lectionis yod and vav) but read plene. Cf. (e.g.) naḥalātēkhā (your inheritance, in numerous places); kohanēkhā (your priests, Ps 132:9 / 2 Chr 6:41); abōtēkhā (your fathers, Gen 31:3 / Jer 34:5 / Prov 22:28); kōḥakhā (thy strength, Judg 16:17); qorbanēkhā (thy offerings, Lev 2:5, 7) — all written without the yod but read with it.[{5}] It is written naʿărāh (girl, defective) but read naʿărâ. It is written, of Lev 12:5, we-ṭāmʿāh shebuʿayim (and she shall be unclean two weeks, with shewa) but read with a shuruq. It is written (1 Sam 5:6, 12): be-ʿōfālīm but read bi-ṭḥōrīm (a euphemism for hemorrhoids). And so for every deficient or surplus letter; for ketib and qere; for the hanging letters — the suspended nun of "Manasseh" in Judg 18:30 (which scribally records the alteration to disguise the original "Moses"); the suspended ʿayin of yaʿar in Ps 80:14; "the wicked" in Job 38:13 and v. 15 with the suspended ʿayin; and so on for what is written but not read, and what is read but not written. The proponent says: the wise know all of this. If a scribe errs by even one letter in a defective or plene spelling, the wise know its proper place, its meaning, and its explanation — to the point that they have counted all the words and all the letters and all the verses and have catalogued them. Anyone who departs from them merits death.

The proponent says: the Mishnah and the Talmud stand to the Torah as a legal document (ṣakk) does to the testimony of its two attesting witnesses: their handwriting matches the document, and no one can dare set their witness aside. So too the wise — they bear witness to the written Torah, and they likewise bear witness to the oral Torah (Torah she-be-ʿal peh). Their testimony reaches from the days of Moses (peace upon him) to the present moment, generation after generation, over the Torah and over the Mishnah and over the Talmud. Who can refute the testimony of all of them? This is reinforced by the words of Moses (Deut 17:10): "Thou shalt do according to the sentence which they shall declare to thee," and (v. 11): "And according to the direction which they shall direct thee." Moreover, God (mighty and exalted) granted the rulings of the wise a status greater than that of the prophets. For He said of the prophets (Deut 18:15): "Accept ye" — after the prophet has manifested a miracle and a sign — whereas of the wise He said (Deut 17:11): "Do as they tell thee" without requiring any miracle at all. The proponent says: these wise men are those whom God (mighty and exalted) approved and chose, and to whom He committed His trust to the end of time. Whoever supposes he can interpret the words of the Torah without the word of the wise — that will not stand. For the Torah has verses that suggest contradiction: e.g., (Deut 16:1) "as He brought thee forth from Egypt by night" vs (Exod 12:51) "on this very day the Lord brought forth all the hosts of Egypt out of the land of Egypt"; (Exod 33:20) "no man shall see Me and live" vs (Isa 6:1) "I saw the Lord" and (Exod 24:10) "and they saw the God of Israel"; (Exod 12:5) "ye shall take it from the sheep or the goats" vs (Deut 16:2) "and thou shalt sacrifice the Passover-offering to the Lord thy God from the herd and the flock." Likewise things whose meaning is opaque: the red heifer (Num 19:2); the sparrows of the metsoraʿ (Lev 14:4); the goat of Azazel (Lev 16:8); Exod 21:22 "he shall pay with equity" (where Scripture has just said "as her husband demands of him"); Deut 17:6 "by the mouth of two witnesses or of three witnesses" (but ordinary speech would put three before two). And the case of the seduced maiden (Exod 22:16): "and if her father refuses to give her to him" — what then happens to the child? Does he give her a ketuba? And what of one who marries a forbidden relation: what is the status of the resulting child? How is the ketuba of children of fornication written? And how is the marriage-document itself written, and the qiddushin — what is the formula? When does the engagement take effect such that, if another man approaches the betrothed, he is to be killed? And how is the ketuba drafted? And Deut 14:11: "every clean bird ye may eat" — we would not know the clean from the unclean without the wise men's explanation in the Mishnah. The proponent goes on: and likewise all the subtleties of practice that are not written down — these we know to honor the excellence of the wise, who transmit them generation by generation; they are not invented in their own hearts. Then he qualifies himself, saying that they "pursue and infer one thing from another." As Solomon ben David (peace upon both of them) said (Prov 22:17): "Incline thine ear and hear the words of the wise." ---
